sections.title: Endgame principles
paras: In the endgame the king becomes a fighting piece. With the queens off the board it is no longer in danger, and it is often the strongest piece you have: bring it toward the centre and toward the pawns.

Passed pawns matter more as material comes off. A passed pawn ties down enemy pieces and can decide the game on its own. The value of the pieces shifts too: rooks grow stronger on open files, and a bishop on an open board can outperform a knight.
Start every endgame by activating your king, creating or stopping passed pawns, and placing rooks behind passed pawns.
sections.key: Activate the king, push or stop passed pawns, and put rooks behind passed pawns.

sections.title: King and pawn endings
paras: King and pawn endings are pure calculation, and they decide many other endings, because a trade of the last pieces can lead straight into one.

The square of the pawn: draw a square from the pawn to its promotion rank. If the defending king can step inside that square on its move, it catches the pawn. The opposition: when the two kings face each other with one square between them, the side that does not have to move holds the opposition, and the other king must give way.
With the king in front of its pawn and on the sixth rank, the attacker wins whoever is to move (except with a rook pawn). Further back, the opposition decides.
sections.key: Use the square to see whether a pawn can be caught, and the opposition to decide whose king must give way.

sections.title: Basic rook endings
paras: Rook endings are the most common endings of all. The guiding rules: keep your rook active rather than tied to passive defense, use it to cut off the enemy king along a rank or file, and place it behind passed pawns, your own or your opponent’s.
A king cut off from a pawn by a rook on a file is often lost for the defender, because the attacking king can escort the pawn without interference.
The training positions put these rules to work.
sections.key: An active rook, the enemy king cut off, and rooks behind passed pawns.

sections.title: Key theoretical positions
paras: Two rook and pawn positions are worth knowing by heart, because so many endings head for them.

In the winning position, the attacker’s king is on the promotion square in front of its own pawn on the seventh rank, and the defending king is cut off. The winning method is to build a bridge: bring the rook to the fourth rank, step the king out, and block the rook checks with the rook.

In the drawing position, the defender keeps the rook on the sixth rank (the third rank from the defender’s side) to stop the attacking king coming forward. Only when the pawn advances to that rank does the rook drop back and check from behind.
sections.key: To win: build a bridge with the rook on the fourth rank. To draw: rook on the third rank until the pawn advances, then checks from behind.

sections.title: Converting an advantage
paras: Winning a won position is a skill of its own. With a queen or rook against a bare king, the method is to restrict the king step by step and drive it to the edge, using your king to support the final mate.

In these practice positions the trainer defends with exact best play from complete endgame tables, so every move you make must keep the win. You have 50 moves to deliver mate, as in the fifty-move rule.
sections.key: Restrict the king, never give stalemate, and bring your own king up for the mate.

items.prompt: White to move. Checkmate with king and queen.
items.explanation: Use the queen to box the king in, a knight’s move away, then bring your king up. Watch for stalemate when the black king has only a few squares.

items.prompt: White to move. Checkmate with king and rook.
items.explanation: Cut the king off with the rook, bring your king up in opposition, and check when the kings face each other. Step by step the box shrinks.
